This isn't a detail-level gap — it's a core-approach change, and it's unflagged, so it's a real finding on both counts.

The plan called for streaming batches specifically to bound memory. Loading everything into memory at once doesn't get to the same guarantee by a different route — it removes the guarantee. Failure mode's different too: a stream-based version degrades or backpressures on a huge export; the load-everything version OOMs the process. That's exactly the kind of thing acceptance criteria won't catch, since they're checking output correctness, not memory behavior under load.

So: passing every criterion doesn't clear it, and nobody flagging the swap means Riley either didn't clock it as a deviation or didn't think it mattered enough to say — either way that's the thing to surface, separate from whether the code itself is otherwise fine.

Before I call it blocking outright, I want the actual reasoning: is there something about the data volume here (e.g., result sets are bounded elsewhere, this export type never gets large) that makes full-memory load actually fine in practice? If so that needs to be said explicitly, on the PR, not assumed. If there isn't a reason like that, this needs to go back — not as a style nit, as a "doesn't do what the plan needed it to do."

Can you get me the actual diff or Riley's own description of why he went this way? I don't want to verdict this off a secondhand summary of the change.
